original_question: If G is an oligomorphic group, must Out(G) = Aut(G)/Inn(G) always be profinite?
target_in_paper: Section 6 (Andre Nies), under "Complexity of isomorphism of oligomorphic groups": Problem 21, "If G is oligomorphic, is Out(G) always profinite?"
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the paper's target almost exactly: it has the correct hypothesis (G oligomorphic), the correct invariant (Out(G)=Aut(G)/Inn(G)), and the correct property being asked about (profinite).
missing_details: In the paper's surrounding context, Aut(G) means the group of continuous automorphisms of the topological group G, not arbitrary abstract automorphisms.
Aut(G) is equipped with a natural Polish topology, supplied immediately before the problem in Theorem 20(1).
Out(G) is considered with the quotient topology, so "profinite" is meant as a topological property of the quotient group.
To make the question stand-alone, one should specify that G is an oligomorphic closed subgroup of Sym(ω), i.e. it has finitely many orbits on ω^n for every n.
The nearby context already proves that Out(G) is totally disconnected and locally compact; the open problem asks whether this can always be strengthened to profinite.
refined_question: Let G be an oligomorphic closed subgroup of Sym(ω). Let Aut(G) denote the group of continuous automorphisms of G, equipped with the natural Polish topology from Theorem 20, and let Out(G)=Aut(G)/Inn(G) be given the quotient topology. Must Out(G) always be a profinite topological group?
justification: This is exactly the official open problem stated in the paper. The only sharpening needed is to import the ambient conventions supplied immediately before it: Theorem 20 makes clear that the relevant automorphism group is the continuous automorphism group with its natural Polish topology, that Inn(G) is closed, and that Out(G) is viewed with the quotient topology. The refined version therefore stays fully faithful to Problem 21 while making explicit the topological meaning of the profiniteness question.
